cases.label: unix epoch 1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z
cases.why: Timestamp 0 is falsy, so `if (!time)` treats a valid date as missing, and west of UTC it is still 1969 locally.

cases.label: 1 ms before the epoch
cases.why: Negative timestamps: `ms % 1000` is -1, not 999, so splitting seconds and milliseconds with % and Math.floor disagree.

cases.label: before 1970 with fractional seconds (1969-12-31T23:59:58.500Z)
cases.why: Truncating -1.5 s toward zero gives 23:59:59 instead of 23:59:58; Math.trunc vs Math.floor and integer division bugs live here.

cases.label: moon landing 1969-07-20T20:17:40.123Z
cases.why: Negative timestamp with milliseconds: serializers that build "seconds.millis" from a negative value print a wrong or doubly negative fraction.

cases.label: local mean time era 1850-01-01T00:00:00Z
cases.why: Before standard time, zones used local mean time with second level offsets (Sao Paulo was -03:06:28); getTimezoneOffset() reports whole minutes, so local arithmetic drifts by seconds.

cases.label: year 0 (0000-01-01T00:00:00Z)
cases.why: Date.UTC(0, 0, 1) and new Date(0, 0, 1) map years 0 to 99 to 1900 to 1999, and toISOString() yields "0000", which "1 BC" formatting must handle.

cases.label: negative year (-000001-01-01T00:00:00Z)
cases.why: toISOString() produces an expanded, signed year "-000001"; regexes that expect four digits reject it.

cases.label: year 2038 limit 2038-01-19T03:14:07Z
cases.why: Last second representable as a signed 32 bit Unix time; anything that stores seconds in an int32 (or uses `| 0`) is fine here.

cases.label: year 2038 overflow 2038-01-19T03:14:08Z
cases.why: One second past the int32 limit: `(ms / 1000) | 0` wraps to 1901-12-13, and so do 32 bit database columns.

cases.label: last instant of year 9999
cases.why: Largest instant with a four digit year; one millisecond later toISOString() switches to "+010000".

cases.label: year 10000 (+010000-01-01T00:00:00.000Z)
cases.why: toISOString() returns a six digit signed year; parsers, databases and YYYY format strings break.

cases.label: maximum Date (+275760-09-13T00:00:00.000Z)
cases.why: Largest valid Date. Adding 1 ms produces Invalid Date, so "end of time" sentinels overflow.

cases.label: minimum Date (-271821-04-20T00:00:00.000Z)
cases.why: Smallest valid Date. Subtracting anything produces Invalid Date, and local offsets west of UTC push the local wall clock out of range.

cases.label: invalid date
cases.why: getTime() is NaN, toISOString() throws RangeError, JSON.stringify gives null and every comparison is false.

cases.label: date-only string parsed as UTC (new Date("2026-03-01"))
cases.why: Date-only ISO strings are UTC midnight, while date-time strings without Z are local; west of UTC this date displays as February 28.

cases.label: leap day 2024-02-29
cases.why: Adding a year with setFullYear(y + 1) lands on 2025-03-01 because Feb 29 2025 does not exist; birthdays and anniversaries drift.

cases.label: leap day 2000-02-29 (400 year rule)
cases.why: 2000 is a leap year because it is divisible by 400, unlike 1900 and 2100; a "divisible by 100 means not leap" rule rejects it.

cases.label: not a leap year 2100-02-28
cases.why: 2100 is not a leap year; `year % 4 === 0` claims Feb 29 2100 exists and the day after this is computed wrong.

cases.label: month end 2026-01-31
cases.why: setMonth(month + 1) on January 31 overflows to March 3, because February 31 does not exist.

cases.label: month end 2026-03-31
cases.why: Adding one month to March 31 gives May 1, since April has 30 days; "same day next month" needs clamping.

cases.label: last millisecond of 2026 (UTC)
cases.why: Range queries ending at 23:59:59 miss this millisecond; month index 11 plus one must roll over into the next year.

cases.label: 2027-01-01 is in ISO week 53 of 2026
cases.why: ISO week years differ from calendar years: this Friday belongs to week 53 of 2026, so `getFullYear()` plus week number is wrong.

cases.label: 2024-12-30 is in ISO week 1 of 2025
cases.why: A Monday in December that belongs to week 1 of the next ISO year; "yyyy-ww" built from the calendar year shows 2024-01.

cases.label: 2023-01-01 is a Sunday in ISO week 52 of 2022
cases.why: ISO weeks start on Monday, US weeks on Sunday: this day is week 52 of 2022 in ISO but week 1 of 2023 in US numbering.

cases.label: America/New_York 2026: 1 ms before spring forward (2026-03-08 01:59 local)
cases.why: Last instant before clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00 (UTC-05:00 to UTC-04:00); adding 60 minutes of wall time here is not 60 minutes of real time.

cases.label: America/New_York 2026: spring forward (2026-03-08 03:00 local)
cases.why: Clocks jump from 02:00 to 03:00; local times in between do not exist, so building a Date from local fields shifts it and that local day is 23 hours long.

cases.label: America/New_York 2026: fall back, first 01:30 (2026-11-01)
cases.why: Clocks fall back from 02:00 to 01:00, so 01:30 happens twice; this is the first one (UTC-04:00). Parsing the local time picks one of the two.

cases.label: America/New_York 2026: fall back, second 01:30 (2026-11-01)
cases.why: Same wall clock reading as the first 01:30, 60 minutes later (UTC-05:00); sorting or deduplicating by local time breaks and that local day is 25 hours long.

cases.label: America/New_York: last instant of 2025 local time
cases.why: Local time is 2025-12-31 23:59:59.999 (UTC-05:00) but the UTC year is already 2026; a year check with getUTCFullYear() is off by one.

cases.label: America/Sao_Paulo 2018: fall back, first 23:30 (2018-02-17)
cases.why: Clocks fall back from 00:00 to 23:00, so 23:30 happens twice; this is the first one (UTC-02:00). Parsing the local time picks one of the two.

cases.label: America/Sao_Paulo 2018: fall back, second 23:30 (2018-02-17)
cases.why: Same wall clock reading as the first 23:30, 60 minutes later (UTC-03:00); sorting or deduplicating by local time breaks and that local day is 25 hours long.

cases.label: America/Sao_Paulo 2018: 1 ms before spring forward (2018-11-03 23:59 local)
cases.why: Last instant before clocks jump from 00:00 to 01:00 (UTC-03:00 to UTC-02:00); adding 60 minutes of wall time here is not 60 minutes of real time.

cases.label: America/Sao_Paulo 2018: spring forward (2018-11-04 01:00 local)
cases.why: Clocks jump from 00:00 to 01:00; local times in between do not exist, so building a Date from local fields shifts it and that local day is 23 hours long. Midnight does not exist that day, so new Date(2018, 10, 4) returns 01:00.

cases.label: America/Sao_Paulo: last instant of 2017 local time
cases.why: Local time is 2017-12-31 23:59:59.999 (UTC-02:00) but the UTC year is already 2018; a year check with getUTCFullYear() is off by one.

cases.label: Europe/London 2026: 1 ms before spring forward (2026-03-29 00:59 local)
cases.why: Last instant before clocks jump from 01:00 to 02:00 (UTC+00:00 to UTC+01:00); adding 60 minutes of wall time here is not 60 minutes of real time.

cases.label: Europe/London 2026: spring forward (2026-03-29 02:00 local)
cases.why: Clocks jump from 01:00 to 02:00; local times in between do not exist, so building a Date from local fields shifts it and that local day is 23 hours long.

cases.label: Europe/London 2026: fall back, first 01:30 (2026-10-25)
cases.why: Clocks fall back from 02:00 to 01:00, so 01:30 happens twice; this is the first one (UTC+01:00). Parsing the local time picks one of the two.

cases.label: Europe/London 2026: fall back, second 01:30 (2026-10-25)
cases.why: Same wall clock reading as the first 01:30, 60 minutes later (UTC+00:00); sorting or deduplicating by local time breaks and that local day is 25 hours long.

cases.label: Australia/Lord_Howe 2026: fall back, first 01:45 (2026-04-05)
cases.why: Clocks fall back from 02:00 to 01:30, so 01:45 happens twice; this is the first one (UTC+11:00). Parsing the local time picks one of the two.

cases.label: Australia/Lord_Howe 2026: fall back, second 01:45 (2026-04-05)
cases.why: Same wall clock reading as the first 01:45, 30 minutes later (UTC+10:30); sorting or deduplicating by local time breaks and that local day is 24.5 hours long.

cases.label: Australia/Lord_Howe 2026: 1 ms before spring forward (2026-10-04 01:59 local)
cases.why: Last instant before clocks jump from 02:00 to 02:30 (UTC+10:30 to UTC+11:00); adding 30 minutes of wall time here is not 30 minutes of real time.

cases.label: Australia/Lord_Howe 2026: spring forward (2026-10-04 02:30 local)
cases.why: Clocks jump from 02:00 to 02:30; local times in between do not exist, so building a Date from local fields shifts it and that local day is 23.5 hours long.

cases.label: Australia/Lord_Howe: first instant of 2026 local time
cases.why: Local time is 2026-01-01 00:00 (UTC+11:00) but the UTC year is still 2025; a year check with getUTCFullYear() is off by one.

cases.label: Asia/Kathmandu: first instant of 2026 local time
cases.why: Local time is 2026-01-01 00:00 (UTC+05:45) but the UTC year is still 2025; a year check with getUTCFullYear() is off by one.

cases.label: Pacific/Kiritimati: first instant of 2026 local time
cases.why: Local time is 2026-01-01 00:00 (UTC+14:00) but the UTC year is still 2025; a year check with getUTCFullYear() is off by one. This zone is among the first places on Earth to enter the new year.

cases.label: Pacific/Pago_Pago: last instant of 2025 local time
cases.why: Local time is 2025-12-31 23:59:59.999 (UTC-11:00) but the UTC year is already 2026; a year check with getUTCFullYear() is off by one. This zone is among the last places on Earth to leave the old year.

cases.label: UTC
cases.why: The control zone: offset 0 all year. Bugs that only show up away from UTC hide here, which is why CI should not run only in UTC.

cases.label: America/New_York
cases.why: UTC-05:00 with US DST rules: the classic negative offset where UTC midnight is the previous local day.

cases.label: America/Los_Angeles
cases.why: UTC-08:00: late enough that evening events land on the next UTC day.

cases.label: America/Sao_Paulo
cases.why: UTC-03:00; used DST with midnight transitions until 2019, so historical dates have days without 00:00.

cases.label: America/St_Johns
cases.why: UTC-03:30: a half hour offset with DST in the Americas; code that assumes whole hours breaks.

cases.label: Europe/London
cases.why: UTC+00:00 in winter but +01:00 in summer: tests that pass in January fail in July.

cases.label: Europe/Dublin
cases.why: The tz database models Irish time with a negative DST save (standard time in summer), which trips code that reads the isDST flag of tz libraries.

cases.label: Africa/Casablanca
cases.why: UTC+01:00 that drops to +00:00 during Ramadan each year, so transitions move with the lunar calendar.

cases.label: Asia/Kolkata
cases.why: UTC+05:30, no DST: the most populous half hour offset.

cases.label: Asia/Kathmandu
cases.why: UTC+05:45: a quarter hour offset that breaks `offset / 60` rounding and hour only offset pickers.

cases.label: Asia/Tehran
cases.why: UTC+03:30; abolished DST in 2022, so historical and current rules differ.

cases.label: Australia/Adelaide
cases.why: UTC+09:30 / +10:30: southern hemisphere DST plus a half hour offset.

cases.label: Australia/Lord_Howe
cases.why: UTC+10:30 / +11:00: DST shifts by only 30 minutes, so "DST adds one hour" is false.

cases.label: Pacific/Chatham
cases.why: UTC+12:45 / +13:45: quarter hour offset with DST, far east of the date line.

cases.label: Pacific/Kiritimati
cases.why: UTC+14:00, the largest offset: local dates are a full day ahead of most of the Americas and the first to reach New Year.

cases.label: Pacific/Apia
cases.why: Samoa skipped 2011-12-30 entirely when it moved across the date line; day counting across that date is off by one.

cases.label: Pacific/Pago_Pago
cases.why: UTC-11:00, among the last places to leave a year; local dates lag a day behind most of Asia.

cases.label: Antarctica/Troll
cases.why: UTC+00:00 in winter and +02:00 in summer: a two hour DST jump.

cases.label: empty string
cases.why: Falsy, length 0: `if (!name)` and `str[0].toUpperCase()` both misbehave.

cases.label: single space
cases.why: Truthy but blank: passes `if (str)` checks and fails after trim().

cases.label: mixed ASCII whitespace
cases.why: Every ASCII whitespace character; trim() returns an empty string but `str.length > 0` validators accept it.

cases.label: no-break space (U+00A0)
cases.why: Arrives from HTML   and copy paste; \s and trim() treat it as whitespace but split(" ") and many tokenizers do not.

cases.label: ideographic space (U+3000)
cases.why: Full width space used in CJK text; trim() removes it, byte based or ASCII only trimming does not.

cases.label: zero width space (U+200B)
cases.why: Invisible and not whitespace for trim() or \s, so it looks identical to "foobar" but is not equal to it.

cases.label: byte order mark prefix (U+FEFF)
cases.why: Left by Windows editors at the start of files: CSV headers become "\uFEFFid" and JSON.parse of BOM prefixed text throws.

cases.label: soft hyphen (U+00AD)
cases.why: Invisible unless a line breaks there, so search and equality fail on text that looks the same.

cases.label: very long string (100000 chars)
cases.why: Exceeds column and header limits, overflows layouts and exposes quadratic algorithms and backtracking regexes.

cases.label: emoji outside the BMP (U+1F600)
cases.why: One visible character but length 2 (a surrogate pair); charAt(0) and str[0] return half of it.

cases.label: ZWJ family emoji (man, woman, girl, boy)
cases.why: Seven code points joined by zero width joiners render as one glyph with length 11; splitting by code point shows four people.

cases.label: flag emoji (regional indicators B and R)
cases.why: A flag is two regional indicator letters; cutting between them leaves letters and reversing them names another country or none.

cases.label: skin tone modifier (thumbs up, medium)
cases.why: Base emoji plus a modifier: one grapheme, two code points, four code units; truncating after the base drops the tone.

cases.label: emoji with variation selector (red heart)
cases.why: U+2764 plus U+FE0F: removing "invisible" characters changes emoji presentation, and the base alone is in the BMP.

cases.label: keycap sequence (digit one)
cases.why: Starts with an ASCII digit, so /^\d/ matches what renders as a single keycap symbol.

cases.label: surrogate pair cut by slice(0, 10)
cases.why: The emoji starts at index 9, so slice(0, 10) keeps only its high surrogate and produces malformed UTF-16.

cases.label: surrogate pair at the end for trimEnd style truncation
cases.why: Truncating "to N code units" from the end lands inside the pair; output ends in a lone surrogate that renders as U+FFFD.

cases.label: lone high surrogate
cases.why: Malformed UTF-16: encodeURIComponent throws URIError, TextEncoder writes U+FFFD and isWellFormed() is false.

cases.label: lone low surrogate
cases.why: A trailing surrogate with no lead: string comparison works but encoding, hashing and JSON round trips through UTF-8 change it.

cases.label: precomposed e acute (NFC)
cases.why: Length 4. Compare with the decomposed form: same rendering, different code points.

cases.label: decomposed e acute (NFD)
cases.why: Length 5 and !== the NFC form; macOS file names and some keyboards produce this form. Use normalize() before comparing.

cases.label: stacked combining marks
cases.why: One base letter with ten combining marks: one grapheme, eleven code units, and rendering that escapes its line box.

cases.label: leading combining mark
cases.why: A combining mark with nothing to attach to; it combines with whatever precedes the string after concatenation.

cases.label: Hangul syllables (precomposed)
cases.why: Korean syllable blocks. NFD splits each into two or three jamo, so lengths change after normalization.

cases.label: Hangul jamo (decomposed)
cases.why: Three jamo that render as one syllable and equal the first syllable of the previous case only after NFC normalization.

cases.label: right to left text mixed with Latin and digits
cases.why: Hebrew mixed with Latin and numbers: visual order differs from memory order, which breaks cursor math and naive truncation with ellipsis.

cases.label: Arabic text
cases.why: Right to left script with contextual letter shapes; per code point styling or splitting breaks the joining.

cases.label: right to left override (U+202E)
cases.why: Displays as "invoiceexe.txt": the Trojan Source trick (CVE-2021-42574) for file names and code review.

cases.label: bidi isolate controls (U+2067, U+2069)
cases.why: Invisible directional isolates change display order; strip or escape them in identifiers and logs.

cases.label: Turkish dotted and dotless i
cases.why: Capital dotted I lowercases to i plus U+0307 (length grows), and toLocaleLowerCase("tr") maps I to dotless i; case insensitive keys break.

cases.label: German sharp s
cases.why: toUpperCase() gives "STRASSE" (length 6 to 7), so upper and lower case comparisons disagree and length based layouts shift.

cases.label: Greek final sigma
cases.why: Lowercasing the whole word yields a final sigma at the end; lowercasing letter by letter does not, so results differ.

cases.label: null character
cases.why: Terminates C strings, is rejected by PostgreSQL text columns and disappears in some loggers.

cases.label: CRLF newline
cases.why: split("\n") leaves a trailing "\r" on each line; Windows files and HTTP headers use this form.

cases.label: CR only newline
cases.why: Classic Mac line ending: code that only looks for \n sees one line.

cases.label: line separator (U+2028)
cases.why: A JavaScript line terminator: `.` in a regex does not match it, and it broke inline scripts and JSONP before ES2019.

cases.label: paragraph separator (U+2029)
cases.why: Another JavaScript line terminator that most text editors render as nothing; line counting tools disagree about it.

cases.label: vertical tab and form feed
cases.why: Rarely seen whitespace that XML 1.0 forbids and some JSON encoders escape inconsistently.

cases.label: HTML markup as text
cases.why: Must render as literal text; any innerHTML or template without escaping executes it.

cases.label: already escaped HTML
cases.why: Escaping twice shows "&lt;" to users; unescaping on input then escaping on output corrupts it.

cases.label: SQL quote and comment
cases.why: A quote ends a string literal in hand built SQL; also tests that names with apostrophes survive a round trip.

cases.label: regex metacharacters
cases.why: Passing user text to new RegExp() throws on "(" or matches everything with ".*"; escape it first.

cases.label: template placeholders
cases.why: Text that looks like template or printf syntax; any second pass through a formatter changes it.

cases.label: __proto__ as a key
cases.why: Used as an object key it sets the prototype instead of a property; use Map or Object.create(null) for user keys.

cases.label: the word null
cases.why: A real surname and a common placeholder: systems that treat "null" as missing lose data.

cases.label: Arabic-Indic digits
cases.why: Unicode digits: Number() and parseInt return NaN and \d only matches ASCII 0 to 9, yet users type these.

cases.label: full width digits
cases.why: Typed by CJK input methods; look like 123 but fail /^\d+$/ and Number().

cases.label: Thai without spaces
cases.why: Thai writes words without spaces and uses combining vowels; word wrapping and counting need Intl.Segmenter.

cases.label: wide CJK characters
cases.why: Each character takes two terminal columns, so padEnd based tables and fixed width output misalign.

cases.label: zero
cases.why: Falsy: `if (!count)` and `value || defaultValue` replace a legitimate 0.

cases.label: negative zero
cases.why: -0 === 0 is true, but Object.is(-0, 0) is false, 1 / -0 is -Infinity and String(-0) is "0", so the sign silently disappears.

cases.label: NaN
cases.why: NaN !== NaN, indexOf cannot find it, JSON.stringify writes null and every comparison is false, so sorting with it is unstable.

cases.label: Infinity
cases.why: JSON.stringify writes null, toFixed returns "Infinity" and a max-age or timeout of Infinity can mean "never" or overflow a timer.

cases.label: -Infinity
cases.why: Math.max() of an empty list; a common reducer seed that leaks into output as "-Infinity".

cases.label: MAX_SAFE_INTEGER
cases.why: 2^53 - 1, the largest integer where n + 1 is exact; IDs and counters past it stop being unique.

cases.label: MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 1
cases.why: 2^53: here n + 1 === n, so loops never advance and 64 bit IDs from JSON collide.

cases.label: MAX_SAFE_INTEGER + 2
cases.why: Is not representable: the literal 9007199254740993 rounds to 9007199254740992 before your code ever sees it.

cases.label: MIN_SAFE_INTEGER
cases.why: -(2^53 - 1), the negative safe integer limit; mirrors the positive overflow bugs.

cases.label: MIN_SAFE_INTEGER - 1
cases.why: First unsafe negative integer: Number.isSafeInteger is false and decrementing it is not exact.

cases.label: MAX_VALUE
cases.why: Largest finite double; doubling it or adding a large value gives Infinity.

cases.label: MIN_VALUE
cases.why: Smallest positive double (5e-324), not the most negative number; code that uses it as "minus infinity" is wrong.

cases.label: EPSILON
cases.why: Gap between 1 and the next double; only meaningful as a tolerance near 1, not for large or tiny values.
Breaks `x | 0` and `x >>> 0` truncation, array index limits and 32 bit counters.
Overflows signed 32 bit math: `(2 ** 31) | 0` is -2147483648.
Between -1 and 0: Math.trunc gives -0, Math.round gives -0, and code that formats the integer part then the fraction drops the minus sign.
A small negative between -1 and 0: formatting with toFixed(2) gives "-0.00", and splitting into integer and fraction parts loses the sign.

cases.label: -1e-7
cases.why: Very small negative: String() gives "-1e-7", so string based number formatting and regexes for digits fail.

cases.label: 1e-7
cases.why: Smallest magnitude where String() switches to exponent notation ("1e-7"), while 0.000001 still prints in full.
0.30000000000000004, not 0.3: exact equality on money and percentages fails; compare with a tolerance or use integers.

cases.label: 0.5 (round half)
cases.why: Math.round(0.5) is 1 but Math.round(-0.5) is -0 and toFixed uses a different rule: half rounding is not symmetric.

cases.label: 1e21
cases.why: First integer where String() uses exponent notation ("1e+21"); toFixed also falls back to exponent form, breaking digit only checks.
Largest round number below 1e21 that still prints all its digits; one step up the format changes.

cases.label: negative integer
cases.why: Modulo keeps the sign (-42 % 5 is -2), so "positive modulo" wraparound for indexes and calendars is wrong.

cases.label: non-integer array index
cases.why: arr[1.5] is undefined and creates a string property on write; Number.isInteger guards are often missing.

cases.label: empty string
cases.why: Number("") is 0, not NaN, so empty form fields become zero.

cases.label: whitespace only
cases.why: Number("  ") is 0 as well; parseFloat returns NaN, so the two parsers disagree.

cases.label: padded number
cases.why: Number trims whitespace and accepts it; strict validators and parseInt with a regex may not.

cases.label: negative zero string
cases.why: Number("-0") is -0, which then prints as "0"; round trips lose the sign.

cases.label: leading zeros
cases.why: Decimal 7 for Number and parseInt, but octal in some legacy parsers and a string ID that must keep its zeros.

cases.label: hex string
cases.why: Number("0x1A") is 26 and parseInt("0x1A") is 26, but parseFloat("0x1A") is 0.

cases.label: binary and octal prefixes
cases.why: Number("0b101") is 5 while parseInt("0b101") is 0; prefixes are accepted by one parser only.

cases.label: exponent notation
cases.why: Number gives 1000 but parseInt gives 1, so "digits only" assumptions break.

cases.label: trailing garbage
cases.why: parseInt and parseFloat return 12, Number returns NaN; lenient parsing hides bad input.

cases.label: comma decimal separator
cases.why: Decimal comma used in most of Europe and Brazil: parseFloat gives 1 and Number gives NaN.

cases.label: thousands separators
cases.why: Grouped digits from formatted output; parseFloat stops at the first comma and returns 1.

cases.label: numeric separator literal
cases.why: Valid in JavaScript source but Number("1_000") is NaN.

cases.label: Infinity string
cases.why: Number("Infinity") is Infinity, so numeric validation accepts a word; JSON cannot represent it.

cases.label: NaN string
cases.why: Number("NaN") is NaN, which passes typeof === "number" checks after conversion.

cases.label: unsafe integer string
cases.why: Parses to 9007199254740992: IDs from JSON or databases silently change; parse as BigInt or keep as string.

cases.label: plus sign
cases.why: Accepted by Number but rejected by many /^\d+$/ validators, and vice versa for UI masks.

cases.label: Arabic-Indic digits
cases.why: Real digits for many users, but Number returns NaN; normalize with Intl or a digit map first.

cases.label: 0n
cases.why: Falsy like 0, and -0n is just 0n (BigInt has no negative zero), so sign preserving code paths diverge from Number.

cases.label: -1n
cases.why: BigInt division truncates toward zero (-1n / 2n is 0n) and % keeps the sign.

cases.label: 2^53 + 1 (first integer Number cannot hold)
cases.why: Number(2n ** 53n + 1n) rounds to 2^53; converting back to Number for math or JSON loses it.

cases.label: int64 max
cases.why: Largest signed 64 bit integer (PostgreSQL bigint, Java long); one more overflows the column.

cases.label: int64 min
cases.why: Smallest signed 64 bit integer; its absolute value does not fit in int64.

cases.label: uint64 max
cases.why: Largest unsigned 64 bit integer; BigInt.asIntN(64, n) turns it into -1n.

cases.label: 2^64 (overflows uint64)
cases.why: Wraps to 0n with BigInt.asUintN(64, n); database drivers reject it.

cases.label: 1e30 as BigInt
cases.why: Far beyond any Number integer: JSON.stringify throws TypeError for any BigInt, and mixing with Number in + throws.

cases.label: localhost with port
cases.why: No dot in the host: "must contain a TLD" validators reject development URLs.

cases.label: credentials in URL
cases.why: Userinfo with an encoded @; naive parsers split on the first @ and leak or mangle the password.

cases.label: IPv6 host with port
cases.why: hostname is "[::1]" with brackets; splitting host and port on ":" breaks.

cases.label: shorthand IPv4 (127.1)
cases.why: The parser normalizes it to 127.0.0.1, so SSRF block lists that compare strings miss it.

cases.label: hex IPv4 (0x7f.0.0.1)
cases.why: Also loopback after normalization; another SSRF filter bypass.

cases.label: internationalized domain
cases.why: hostname becomes punycode ("xn--r8jz45g.jp"), so comparing the input string with url.hostname fails.

cases.label: trailing dot in host
cases.why: A fully qualified name that is a different origin from example.com for cookies, CORS and allow lists.

cases.label: uppercase scheme and host
cases.why: Scheme and host are lowercased but the path keeps its case; string compares of URLs disagree with the parser.

cases.label: explicit default port
cases.why: url.port is "" because the default port is dropped; code expecting "443" breaks.

cases.label: port out of range
cases.why: Ports above 65535 make the URL invalid; regex validators accept any digits.

cases.label: encoded slash in path
cases.why: Servers and routers disagree on whether %2F is a path separator; decode once at the right layer.

cases.label: plus and space in query
cases.why: URLSearchParams decodes "+" as a space but decodeURIComponent does not; the key also repeats.

cases.label: double encoded space
cases.why: Decoding twice turns %2520 into a space; decoding once gives "%20" literally.

cases.label: empty fragment
cases.why: url.hash is "" even though href ends with "#", so hash based checks see no fragment.

cases.label: dot segments in path
cases.why: Normalized to /secret by the parser; checks done on the raw string allow traversal.

cases.label: non ASCII path and query
cases.why: The parser percent encodes both as UTF-8, so href no longer equals the input.

cases.label: very long URL (8000 char path)
cases.why: Exceeds common 2048 character limits and 8 KB request line limits in proxies and servers.

cases.label: javascript: scheme
cases.why: A valid URL that runs code when used as an href; allow list schemes instead of block listing.

cases.label: javascript: with a newline inside
cases.why: The parser removes tabs and newlines, so this is javascript:alert(1); block lists that match the raw string miss it.

cases.label: data: URL with HTML
cases.why: Valid and executable in some contexts; never forward user supplied data URLs to href or src.

cases.label: file URL with Windows drive
cases.why: host is empty and pathname is "/C:/Windows/win.ini" with a leading slash before the drive letter.

cases.label: mailto URL
cases.why: No host at all: url.host is "" and url.origin is "null".

cases.label: surrounding spaces
cases.why: The parser strips leading and trailing spaces, so it is valid, but the stored string is not.

cases.label: protocol relative
cases.why: Invalid without a base, but resolves to another host with one: "starts with /" open redirect checks pass it.

cases.label: backslash relative
cases.why: Browsers treat "\" as "/" in http URLs, so this resolves to //example.com: a classic open redirect.

cases.label: bare domain without scheme
cases.why: What users type, but not a URL: new URL throws and links become relative paths.

cases.label: space in host
cases.why: Forbidden host code point; new URL throws.

cases.label: empty string
cases.why: new URL("") throws; optional URL fields must be checked before parsing.

cases.label: plus addressing
cases.why: Gmail and others deliver it to "user"; validators that reject "+" lose real users.

cases.label: dots in local part
cases.why: Valid and common; some providers ignore the dots, so deduplication by string misses duplicates.

cases.label: apostrophe in local part
cases.why: Valid; breaks SQL built by concatenation and regexes limited to [a-z0-9._].

cases.label: quoted local part with space
cases.why: A quoted string may contain spaces; nearly every regex rejects it and naive splitting on spaces breaks.

cases.label: quoted local part with @
cases.why: Splitting on the first "@" yields the wrong domain; use the last "@".

cases.label: IP address literal domain
cases.why: Domain literal in brackets; DNS based checks and domain allow lists do not expect it.

cases.label: dotless domain
cases.why: Valid syntax used on intranets and in tests, rejected by "needs a TLD" rules.

cases.label: uppercase address
cases.why: Domains are case insensitive, local parts technically are not; lowercasing everything can merge different mailboxes, not lowercasing creates duplicates.

cases.label: subdomains and long TLD
cases.why: Multi label domains and two part public suffixes; "last two labels" logic picks co.uk.

cases.label: new generic TLD
cases.why: TLDs longer than 4 letters exist; {2,4} quantifiers reject them.

cases.label: shortest realistic address
cases.why: Single character local part and short domain; minimum length rules are often too strict.

cases.label: 64 character local part (maximum)
cases.why: The longest local part RFC 5321 allows; storage columns sized at 50 truncate it.

cases.label: internationalized local part
cases.why: Valid with SMTPUTF8 (RFC 6531) but rejected by ASCII only servers; decide explicitly what you accept.

cases.label: internationalized domain
cases.why: The domain must be converted to punycode for DNS and SMTP; comparing raw strings fails.

cases.label: 65 character local part (too long)
cases.why: One over the RFC 5321 limit; lenient validators accept it and the SMTP server rejects it later.

cases.label: missing @
cases.why: No separator at all; code that splits on "@" gets one part and reads undefined.

cases.label: missing local part
cases.why: Empty local part; split("@")[0] is "".

cases.label: missing domain
cases.why: Empty domain; split("@")[1] is "".

cases.label: two @ signs
cases.why: Unquoted second "@" is invalid; splitting gives three parts.

cases.label: leading dot
cases.why: A dot may not start the local part.

cases.label: trailing dot in local part
cases.why: A dot may not end the local part (some providers accept it anyway).

cases.label: consecutive dots
cases.why: Consecutive dots are not allowed unquoted.

cases.label: consecutive dots in domain
cases.why: Empty domain label; DNS lookups fail.

cases.label: domain label starting with hyphen
cases.why: Host labels may not start with a hyphen.

cases.label: unquoted space
cases.why: Spaces need quoting; forms that do not trim also produce trailing spaces.

cases.label: display name format
cases.why: A valid mailbox header, not a bare address; pasted from mail clients into address fields.

cases.label: Windows absolute path
cases.why: Backslash separators: splitting on "/" returns one segment, and on POSIX this is a relative file name containing backslashes.

cases.label: Windows path with forward slashes
cases.why: Windows accepts it, path.win32 understands it, path.posix treats it as relative.

cases.label: drive relative path
cases.why: Relative to the current directory of drive C, not the root; path.win32.isAbsolute returns false.

cases.label: root relative on Windows
cases.why: Absolute on the current drive only; the result depends on process.cwd() drive.

cases.label: UNC share path
cases.why: Starts with two backslashes; the "root" is \\server\share\, so dirname and parent walking stop there.

cases.label: long path prefix
cases.why: Disables normalization: "/" is not a separator and ".." is literal; needed beyond 260 characters.

cases.label: path longer than 260 characters
cases.why: Exceeds the classic MAX_PATH limit; many Windows tools fail without long path support.

cases.label: reserved device name
cases.why: CON, PRN, AUX, NUL, COM1 and LPT1 cannot be file names on Windows, with any extension.

cases.label: reserved name with extension
cases.why: Still the AUX device on Windows; repositories with this file cannot be checked out there.

cases.label: trailing dot
cases.why: Windows strips trailing dots, so "file." and "file" are the same file there but different on POSIX.

cases.label: trailing space
cases.why: Windows strips trailing spaces as well; invisible in most UIs.

cases.label: case only difference
cases.why: Case insensitive on default Windows and macOS file systems, so readme.md and README.md collide.

cases.label: POSIX absolute path
cases.why: Absolute on POSIX; on Windows path.win32 treats it as root relative on the current drive.

cases.label: trailing slash
cases.why: basename("dir/sub/") is "sub", but split("/").pop() is ""; joining adds a double slash.

cases.label: repeated slashes
cases.why: Equivalent to /a/b/c after normalization; string comparisons and cache keys disagree.

cases.label: root only
cases.why: dirname("/") is "/" and basename is ""; loops that walk up until dirname changes must stop here.

cases.label: empty path
cases.why: path.join("", "") is "." and path.resolve("") is the cwd; empty is not "no path".

cases.label: current directory
cases.why: A path that refers to the cwd; extname(".") is "" and basename is ".".

cases.label: parent directory traversal
cases.why: Escapes the base directory after join; validate with path.relative after resolving.

cases.label: traversal hidden inside a path
cases.why: Looks rooted in uploads/ but normalizes outside it.

cases.label: Windows traversal with backslashes
cases.why: Checks that only look for "../" miss backslash traversal on Windows.

cases.label: dotfile
cases.why: extname(".env") is "", not ".env"; hidden on POSIX and easy to leak in static servers.

cases.label: double extension
cases.why: extname gives ".gz"; type detection and "strip the extension" give "archive.tar".

cases.label: spaces in names
cases.why: Breaks unquoted shell commands and URL building without encoding.

cases.label: backslash in a POSIX file name
cases.why: A legal single file name on Linux that becomes two segments on Windows.

cases.label: NFC unicode name
cases.why: Precomposed form, as typed on Windows and Linux.

cases.label: NFD unicode name
cases.why: Decomposed form produced by older macOS file systems; looks the same as the NFC name but does not match it.

cases.label: emoji in file name
cases.why: Surrogate pairs in a path: byte limits, truncation and some archive tools mishandle them.

cases.label: leading dash
cases.why: Interpreted as an option by command line tools unless passed after "--".

cases.label: newline in file name
cases.why: Legal on Linux; breaks line based tools such as `find | xargs` and log parsing.

cases.label: deeply nested arrays (10000 levels)
cases.why: Valid JSON that overflows the stack of recursive walkers, deep equality checks and schema validators.

cases.label: deeply nested objects (10000 levels)
cases.why: Same as nested arrays for code that recurses into object values, such as deep merge and clone helpers.

cases.label: duplicate keys
cases.why: Allowed by JSON.parse, which keeps the last value; other parsers keep the first or reject it, so validators and consumers disagree.

cases.label: integer above 2^53
cases.why: Parses to 9007199254740992: IDs silently change. Send large IDs as strings.

cases.label: huge exponent
cases.why: Valid JSON that parses to Infinity, which JSON.stringify then writes as null.

cases.label: negative zero
cases.why: Parses to -0, but JSON.stringify(-0) is "0", so round trips lose the sign.

cases.label: number with trailing zeros
cases.why: Parses to 1 and stringifies as "1": signatures and hashes over JSON text change after a round trip.

cases.label: __proto__ key
cases.why: JSON.parse creates an own property, but merging the result into another object with assignment pollutes its prototype.

cases.label: empty key
cases.why: Valid; path based libraries (a.b.c syntax) cannot address it.

cases.label: escaped lone surrogate
cases.why: Valid JSON that decodes to malformed UTF-16; re-encoding to UTF-8 or a database fails.

cases.label: line and paragraph separators
cases.why: Valid JSON that was invalid in JavaScript string literals before ES2019, which broke JSONP and inline script tags.

cases.label: top level string
cases.why: Valid JSON since RFC 7159; code that assumes an object reads properties of a string.

cases.label: top level null
cases.why: Valid JSON that parses to null; `const { a } = JSON.parse(text)` throws.

cases.label: whitespace around value
cases.why: Valid; byte or regex based detectors that check the first character for "{" fail.

cases.label: byte order mark prefix
cases.why: Windows tools write a BOM; JSON.parse throws on it, so strip it when reading files.

cases.label: trailing comma
cases.why: Accepted by JavaScript and JSON5, rejected by JSON.parse.

cases.label: comments
cases.why: Common in config files (JSONC) but invalid JSON.

cases.label: single quotes
cases.why: JavaScript object syntax, not JSON.

cases.label: NaN literal
cases.why: Python json.dumps writes NaN by default, and JSON.parse rejects it.

cases.label: unquoted key
cases.why: JavaScript object literal syntax that JSON does not allow.

cases.label: empty text
cases.why: An empty response body is not JSON; JSON.parse("") throws "Unexpected end of JSON input".

cases.label: raw control character in string
cases.why: Unescaped tab inside a string is invalid JSON even though it looks harmless.

cases.label: empty array
cases.why: Truthy even though empty; reduce without a seed throws and Math.max(...[]) is -Infinity.

cases.label: array with a hole
cases.why: forEach, map and filter skip the hole but for...of and spread yield undefined, so the two styles disagree.

cases.label: explicit undefined
cases.why: Looks like the hole case when printed, but every iteration method visits it and `1 in arr` is true.

cases.label: length 5 with no elements
cases.why: new Array(5) has five holes: map returns holes, not values, and JSON.stringify writes nulls.

cases.label: huge sparse length (2^32 - 1)
cases.why: The maximum array length: cheap to create, but any loop to length or Array.from runs four billion times.

cases.label: NaN element
cases.why: indexOf(NaN) is -1 while includes(NaN) is true; Set and Map treat NaN as equal to itself.

cases.label: -0 and 0
cases.why: Set collapses them into one value and includes(-0) finds 0; Object.is tells them apart.

cases.label: numbers that sort as strings
cases.why: Default sort() compares strings, giving [1, 10, 100, 9]; always pass a comparator.

cases.label: undefined during sort
cases.why: sort() moves undefined to the end without calling the comparator, so comparators never see it.

cases.label: mixed number and numeric string
cases.why: includes("1") and Set treat them as different, while == and loose lookups do not.

cases.label: nested empty arrays
cases.why: flat() and recursive flatten helpers must handle empty levels; String([[[]]]) is "".

cases.label: array with extra property
cases.why: for...in visits "extra" and Object.keys includes it, but length and JSON.stringify ignore it.

cases.label: frozen array
cases.why: push and in place sort throw TypeError in strict mode; libraries that mutate input break.

cases.label: 500000 elements (too many to spread)
cases.why: Math.max(...arr) and fn.apply(null, arr) exceed the argument limit and throw RangeError.
